genZNote: Bigger oocysts than Cryptosporidium, and — unusually for a diarrheal pathogen — it comes with peripheral eosinophilia.

morphology.size: Oocysts ~20-30 x 10-19 µm — notably larger than Cryptosporidium or Cyclospora oocysts

protozoanDetails.lifeCycleForm: Oocyst (initially containing one sporoblast, later two sporocysts each with four sporozoites once mature)

habitat.hostAssociation: Obligate human pathogen — no significant animal reservoir, unlike Cryptosporidium
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Oocysts shed in stool require time in the environment to mature (sporulate) before becoming infectious

microscopy.appearance: Large, ellipsoidal, acid-fast oocysts, distinctly larger than Cryptosporidium oocysts

identificationClues: Large, ellipsoidal, acid-fast oocysts on modified acid-fast stool stain — notably larger than Cryptosporidium's round oocysts
Eosinophilia is common, unlike most other causes of infectious diarrhea
Classic cause of prolonged, severe diarrhea in advanced HIV/AIDS

diseases: Cystoisosporiasis (isosporiasis) — watery diarrhea, can become chronic and severe in immunocompromised hosts
clinicalImportance.transmission: Fecal-oral, via ingestion of sporulated (mature) oocysts in contaminated food or water
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: An important opportunistic cause of chronic diarrhea in people with advanced HIV/AIDS, particularly in tropical/subtropical regions
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Oocyst size and acid-fast staining pattern distinguish it from Cryptosporidium and Cyclospora on the same modified acid-fast stool preparation; associated eosinophilia is a useful supporting clue

examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Larger oocysts than Cryptosporidium; associated with peripheral eosinophilia, unusual among diarrheal pathogens
